finding: §4.2.1 makes 'A unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty' load-bearing — it is what keeps hooks/stop-role-incomplete.sh from refusing the unit's first stop — and closes the paragraph with 'no hook change is needed, only the instruction'. But the spec never names a channel that can carry that instruction, and every candidate is closed by the spec's own rules: (a) there is no prompt in this case by definition, so prompts[].prompt cannot carry it; (b) review_loop.instruction cannot, because §6.2 property 12 requires the --role form to be a *sentence-subset* of the unrestricted instruction, and the unrestricted instruction contains no such sentence — measured on this round's payload it is exactly 6 sentences (spawn a sub-agent / merge+record / repeat until --status --check / read the spec / regression ordering / uncounted delta pass), none about writing an empty file, so no subset can introduce it; (c) tp audit emits no review_loop key at all, yet §4.2.1's rule is stated for both commands. The implementer is left to invent a new top-level key or a new prompt-shaped object, which is schema surface Non-Goal 7 says is untouched.
suggestion: Name the channel explicitly. The cheapest option that does not fight property 12 is a dedicated top-level key on the empty-prompts payload (e.g. `unit_instruction` or reusing `skipped_roles[].reason` plus a fixed hint string), stated in §4.2.1 and given its own property in §6.2.2 — and Non-Goal 7 amended to name it alongside the two clauses and review_loop.instruction. If instead the intent is that the *brief* (§4.2.3) carries it, say so in §4.2.1 and make it a clause of the brief rather than of the payload.

finding: Property 10 requires that each role unit's brief_command, 'running it, exits 0'. §4.2.3 fixes the audit-role brief as `tp audit <spec> --role <id>` with no other flag. §7 of this same spec measures that in a clean git repository `tp audit <spec>` exits **4** with 'no changed files detected (staged+unstaged is empty)' — it 'does not pass vacuously, it does not run at all'. So for every audit-role unit, property 10 is false in exactly the tree state §7 says is normal at gate time, and the property pins no environment that would make it true. The two statements cannot both be satisfied by one implementation: §7's own remedy (supply `--affected-files` or `--base <previous tag>`) is prescribed for the gate only and is absent from the brief §4.2.3 specifies.
suggestion: Either scope property 10 to an environment ('in a tree where the command's own preconditions are met — for tp audit, a non-empty changed-file set'), or make §4.2.3's audit brief carry what tp audit needs (the driver knows the base; `tp audit <spec> --role <id> --base <ref>`). Whichever is chosen, state it in §4.2.3 as well, since the brief is also the interactive path's instruction and an operator running it on a clean tree gets exit 4 with no indication that the brief was incomplete.

finding: §1, §1.1 and §2.1 each state without qualification that on the `tp run` path §2's constraint is already enforced by a fence, and §2.2 reverses that claim in the same document while none of the three is updated. §1: "Under `tp run` §2's constraint is already a fence (§2.1) and §3's salvage is already refused by the driver (§3.1), so on that path the two clauses are belt-and-braces rather than the mechanism." §1.1: "The clauses are emitted on every path, including the one where §2's constraint is already enforced by a fence." §2.1: "Under `tp run` the clause therefore restates a rule the fence already enforces — which is why §1 prices it rather than claiming it." §2.2 then: "Both hooks match tool calls; a state write performed inside a `tp` subprocess is not one. So on the `tp run` path the clause is not purely belt-and-braces after all — it is the only statement about a write channel the fence cannot see." Both cannot be true, and the paragraph carrying the error is the one §1 introduces as "stated up front because it is not uniform" — the release's own account of where the benefit lands. Non-Goal 4 inherits it: it names only "the interactive path" as the place the isolation constraint is unenforced, whereas on §2.2's reading the subprocess channel is unfenced on both paths, so the release leaves more unenforced than its Non-Goal admits.
suggestion: Settle fence reach once, in §2.1, and have §1, §1.1 and Non-Goal 4 read from it rather than restate it. If §2.2 is right: §1 should say the clauses are belt-and-braces on the `tp run` path *for tool-call writes only* and load-bearing for the subprocess channel on both paths, and Non-Goal 4 should be re-scoped from "the interactive path" to "the write channel no PreToolUse hook can see". If §2.2 is wrong, delete its third paragraph — four statements of the same fact with one reversal and no reconciliation is the drift §1.1 already records four retired rules for.

finding: §4.2.3.1 plus §6.2 property 12 buy a `review_loop.instruction` value that is measurably empty or one stale sentence, and the spec never says which. Measured on this round's own emission (round 15, this spec): the key is 592 bytes in six sentences — spawn-a-sub-agent; merge/verify/resolve/record; repeat-until-`--status --check`-exits-0; 'Read the spec at <path> before processing each prompt'; process-regression-first; and the uncounted `--perspective regression` delta pass. Five are orchestrator-addressed by §4.2.3.1's own rule (they direct merging, recording, looping and regression ordering, none of which a single-prompt caller does). The sixth is itself panel-worded — 'each prompt' — and property 12 fixes the transform as a sentence-*subset*, so it cannot be reworded to be true. The honest output is therefore `instruction: ""` or one sentence carrying a false plural. For that yield the release spends a 35-line spec section, a numbered property, and a task-owned fixture whose job is deciding which sentences are orchestrator-addressed — and §4.2.3.1 states no value for the empty-subset case, so a consumer cannot distinguish an empty string from a broken emitter.
suggestion: Replace the subset rule with omission: under `--role`, omit the `review_loop.instruction` member entirely and leave `review_loop`'s other members alone. That is one branch at the emission site instead of a fixture that must be re-read every time a sentence is added at one of `buildReviewLoopInstruction`'s nine assignment sites; it cannot drift, it satisfies §4.2.3.1's rule vacuously ('no sentence directs an unsupported action' is trivially true of no sentences), and 'the key is absent' is unambiguous where '' is not. If the key must remain present, §4.2.3.1 has to state its value when no sentence survives the subset.

finding: §4.2.3.1's rewritten premise this round is that the `--role` payload holds one prompt, and §4.2.1 mandates a `--role` payload that holds none. §4.2.3.1: "Under `--role` the payload holds one prompt and no regression prompt, so the instruction directs actions that payload cannot support", under the headline "The rule turns on the payload, not on who is calling" — so after this round's repair the payload's cardinality is the rule's entire basis. §4.2.1: a name tp recognises but the round does not emit "exits 0 with `prompts: []`". That branch is not a corner case the rule can ignore; §4.2.1 says it is "forced by the driver", because a corpus role skipped `no-checklist-items` or `no-spec-change` is still spawned as a unit (the two bold rows of §4.2.1's own table) and §4.2.3 makes that unit's first command `tp review <spec> --role <id>` — which lands exactly on the empty payload. So the rule's stated basis omits a case the release requires to exist and requires to finish cleanly. It is not a wording nit: a one-prompt payload can still support directives like "read your prompt" and "write your findings file", a zero-prompt payload supports neither, so the blockquote rule selects different sentence sets in the two cases and §4.2.3.1 names only one. Property 12 is stated over all of `--role` and so inherits the gap.
suggestion: State the premise over both payloads the release permits — "Under `--role` the payload holds at most one prompt and no regression prompt" — and say what `review_loop.instruction` is in the `prompts: []` case, since §4.2.1 requires a unit to reach that branch, exit 0 and still write its (empty) findings file. If the answer is that the key is emptied there, say so, because §6.2 property 12 currently has no lower bound and would accept it silently.

finding: §7's new paragraph this round withdraws the premise §6.1 uses to bound every isolation solution, and §6.1 was not updated — so the two sections derive opposite requirements from the same invocation. §6.1 S1: "Two constraints bound any solution: `--no-state` is not one … and relocating the state means relocating the spec, since `engine.ReviewStateDir` derives the directory from the spec's own path with no override, while the `tp audit` half needs a working tree with git history because it detects affected files by `git diff`." §7, added this round: "Measured in a clean git repository, `tp audit <spec>` exits 4 with `no changed files detected (staged+unstaged is empty)` … The gate supplies them with `--affected-files` or `--base <previous tag>`; which one is the implementer's." The gate is §6.2 property 8 and S1 is stated over the suite as a whole, so both govern the same audit invocation. Under `--affected-files` that invocation runs no `git diff` and needs no history at all — S1's second bound simply does not hold, and an isolation S1's wording rules out (a bare temporary tree with no git objects) becomes available. Under `--base <previous tag>` it needs history *and* a reachable tag, which is strictly stronger than S1 states. §7 explicitly declines to choose between them, so S1 asserts one unconditional bound that is false in one branch and understated in the other, and two engineers reading §6.1 plus §7 provision different trees.
suggestion: Give the choice one owner. Either move it into S1 — "the `tp audit` half needs affected files, and how the suite supplies them (`--affected-files` vs `--base <tag>`) decides whether it also needs git history and tags" — or, if §7 keeps the choice, replace S1's `git diff` clause with the weaker fact that survives both branches (the audit half needs a git working tree because §7's gate runs it in one) and cross-reference §7 for the rest.

finding: Property 3 asserts more about the strip than §2.3 and §1.1 specify, and on a body ending in two newlines the two cannot both be satisfied. §2.3 and §1.1 fix the strip as exactly one byte ("trailing newline removed", table row "−1"). Property 3 asserts that the body minus its last 468 bytes "does **not** end with a newline". For a pre-append body ending in LF LF, the spec-conforming implementation (remove one) leaves a remainder that ends with a newline, so property 3 goes red against a correct implementation; the implementation that passes property 3 must strip every trailing newline, which falsifies §1.1's −1 row and its +467 net delta for that prompt. Nothing in §6.1 or §6.2 forbids a body ending in two newlines — §1.1's "every role prompt body ends with \\n" is a measurement of one round's emission, not a constraint the implementation controls, and the body is assembled from spec text whose trailing whitespace the spec under review chooses. Two engineers therefore write contradictory strips (TrimSuffix vs TrimRight) and contradictory assertions, and both can cite the spec.
suggestion: Pin the quantifier once, in §2.3, and make property 3 restate it rather than imply a stronger one: either "exactly one trailing newline is removed, if present" — in which case property 3's second clause becomes "the remainder does not end with LF LF" — or "all trailing newlines are removed", in which case §1.1's −1 row must be relabelled as the measured value for a body ending in a single newline and the +467 net delta stamped as conditional on it.

finding: Property 4's key-invariance rule is explicitly scoped to one of the three name classes, so the exit-0 class — the one §4.2.1 says the driver forces the release to have — has no rule for any key except `prompts`. Property 4 opens "**When `<name>` is in the emitted set**" and only then says "Every other top-level key is unchanged, and `review_loop` is unchanged except its `instruction` member". Property 5 covers the other class and constrains exactly two things: exit 0, and `prompts: []`, plus an echo of the reason in the default mode. Nothing states what the exit-0 payload does with `skipped_roles` itself, and §4.2.1's wording is the ambiguity in one sentence: "the role's own entry present in `skipped_roles`" reads equally as "skipped_roles is unchanged and happens to contain it" and as "skipped_roles is reduced to that entry". Measured on this spec at round 15 the default payload carries `skipped_roles: []`, so the live corpus cannot settle it either. Two engineers write opposite assertions (`len(skipped_roles)==1` vs `skipped_roles` deep-equal to the unrestricted payload's), both pass their own implementation, and `spec_ref`, `structured_elements` and `review_loop`'s non-instruction members are unasserted in this branch by either engineer.
suggestion: Give property 5 the same key-invariance sentence property 4 has, stated for its own class: "Every top-level key except `prompts` is unchanged from the otherwise identical invocation without the flag — including `skipped_roles`, which retains every entry — and `review_loop` is unchanged except its `instruction` member (property 12)." Then §4.2.1 can drop "the role's own entry present in" and say only that the reason is the one `skipped_roles` already carries.

finding: Property 11 asserts 'The emitted role set minus the unit set is exactly {regression}' as a set equality, but never says which invocation produces 'the emitted role set'. §4.2.2 legalises --role — and therefore emission — in `--perspective` and `--verify` as well as the default mode, and §4.3 states `--perspective` has 'its own prompt builder': under `--perspective testing` the emitted set is {test-planner}, which §4.2 says is 'in neither' the corpus nor the unit set, so emitted-minus-unit is {test-planner}, not {regression}. Under `--verify` it is the verify prompt's role. An implementer writing this test must guess the invocation, and the two plausible guesses give opposite verdicts; because §7 makes property 8 (hence the property family) the release gate, guessing wrong either blocks a correct release or passes a broken one.
suggestion: Qualify property 11 with its invocation the way property 5 qualifies its modes: 'For the default mode of each command, at a round where regression emits, the emitted role set minus the unit set is exactly {regression}.' If the property is also meant to hold under --perspective/--verify, state the expected difference set for those modes explicitly rather than leaving the quantifier open.

finding: Property 11 is stated with a precondition the suite is forbidden from creating and a subject it never names, so no deterministic test can be written from it. It reads: "The emitted role set minus the unit set is exactly `{regression}` **at a round where `regression` emits**, as set equality." §4.1 fixes when `regression` emits — from round 2 onward, and only when the spec has changed since the round's snapshot or a finding carries a `fixed` disposition — all of which live in `spec/.tp-review/<base>/`, which S1 forbids the suite from mutating and §6.1 says cannot be relocated without relocating the spec. So the test cannot construct its own precondition; it can only hunt the live tree for a spec that currently satisfies it, which is exactly the state-encoded fixture S2 forbids and which flips as rounds are recorded. Property 11 also names no spec and no command, and the unit set is only non-empty where a task file exists and the phase is review — measured, 15 of the 22 version specs have a `.tasks.json` — so on the other 7 the set difference is the whole emitted role set and the property is simply false, with nothing in the text to exclude them.
suggestion: Name the subject and make the precondition observable rather than arranged: "For a spec whose current emission includes a `regression` prompt (observed on the payload, not arranged by the test), `tp review`'s emitted role set minus `engine.BuildNextUnits`' role-unit set equals `{regression}`; where no `regression` prompt is emitted the two sets are equal. Evaluated only on specs for which the review phase produces role units." That is decidable from one emission plus one unit derivation, with no state the suite has to create.

finding: Property 12 fixes the --role instruction as containing 'none of that key's orchestrator-addressed directives'. §4.2.3.1 explicitly rejects that criterion in this same release: 'The rule turns on the payload, not on who is calling. A draft grounded it on the caller being "a unit, not the orchestrator", which §4.3 falsifies in the same release — a human orchestrator invokes --role once per role, and nothing in the flag distinguishes the two.' §4.2.3.1's surviving rule is payload-supportability ('no sentence may direct an action the caller's own payload cannot support'). The two predicates are not equivalent and can disagree on a real sentence: 'Read the spec at <path> before processing each prompt' is orchestrator-addressed in origin yet perfectly supportable by a single-prompt payload. The implementer therefore has two different acceptance tests for one edit, and §6 says the properties are 'what an implementation must satisfy'.
suggestion: Restate property 12 in §4.2.3.1's own vocabulary: 'Under --role, review_loop.instruction is a sentence-subset of the unrestricted one and contains no sentence directing an action the single-prompt payload cannot support. Without --role it is unchanged.' Then the trailing note ('which sentences are orchestrator-addressed is a fixture the task owns') should also be rewritten in terms of supportability, or dropped — it currently hands the task a fixture keyed on the abandoned criterion.

finding: The spec's rejected-draft narration is now a third of the document and it sits inline in the normative text, where it is paid every round by every role. Measured: 15,858 of 46,990 bytes (33.7%), spread over 23 of the document's 129 blank-line-separated blocks (blocks matching 'a draft' / 'an earlier draft' / 'drafts'). §1.1 alone gives seven lines to a retired index and a retired naming rule; §2.2, §2.3, §3.1, §4.2.1, §4.2.3, §4.2.3.1, §6.2.1, §6.2.2 and §7 each carry their own. Every role prompt tells the unit to read the spec file before reviewing, and tp embeds changed sections verbatim into the prompt, so that third is multiplied by roles and by rounds — this cycle is at round 15. The content itself is worth keeping and this spec is right that a recorded dead end is what stops it being re-proposed; the cost is the placement, because an implementer reading for what must be true has no way to skip what used to be true.
suggestion: Apply §6.3's own pattern to the rest of the document. §6.3 already demonstrates the cheap shape — one `Withdrawn | Why` table, out of line, so 'the properties stay readable and the reasons stay found'. Promote it to a release-level section (or one such table per major section) and leave the normative paragraphs stating only the rule and its measurement. No dead end is lost, cross-references still resolve, and the text every role must read each round drops by roughly a third.

finding:
§2.3's construction opens with '<the body as assembled before this release's append, trailing newline removed>' and §1.1 prices it at exactly −1, but neither says whether the implementer strips *one* trailing newline or *all* of them. The distinction is made load-bearing by §6.2 property 3, whose second half asserts that the body with its last 468 bytes removed 'does not end with a newline': under strip-one that assertion holds only if the pre-existing body ends with exactly one LF, which is a property of a builder this release does not otherwise touch. §1.1's supporting measurement is stated as 'every role prompt body ends with 
', which does not exclude a body ending with 

. Measured on this round's own emission all five bodies do end with exactly one LF, so the ambiguity is latent rather than live — but the implementer must still commit to a construction, and the two choices diverge silently the first time any prompt builder emits a trailing blank line.
suggestion: Make the arity explicit in §2.3 — 'all trailing newlines removed' is the choice that makes property 3 true of the emitter rather than of an upstream builder, and it keeps §1.1's −1 correct for the measured case. If strip-one is intended instead, add the precondition to §1.1 ('every prompt body ends with exactly one LF') so property 3's second clause has a stated basis rather than an incidental one.

finding: In the exit-0 branch (a name tp recognises that the round does not emit) §4.2.1 requires 'prompts: []' and 'the role's own entry present in skipped_roles'. 'Present in' constrains presence only, so it does not say whether skipped_roles is *filtered* to that one entry — mirroring what --role does to prompts[] — or left carrying the whole panel's skipped roles. The in-emitted-set branch is pinned in the opposite direction: §6.2 property 4 says 'every other top-level key is unchanged', so there skipped_roles keeps all its entries. An implementer reading both naturally infers symmetry (filter prompts[], filter skipped_roles) and would then violate property 4; reading property 4 alone infers no filtering anywhere and leaves §4.2.1's 'the role's own entry' as an accident of the unfiltered list. Nothing decides it, and the choice is observable to any caller that reads skipped_roles to learn why it got nothing.
suggestion: State it once in §4.2.1: '--role filters prompts[] only; skipped_roles is unchanged, and the named role's entry is located within it' (or the filtering alternative, if that is the intent) — and, if filtering is chosen, add the exception to property 4's 'every other top-level key is unchanged' the same way review_loop.instruction is excepted.

finding: §4.2.1 spends three paragraphs, an exit-0 branch and an 'a unit that receives no prompt still creates its findings file, empty' instruction making a unit that provably emits no prompt finish cleanly — but never asks whether that unit should be spawned at all. Its own skip table says `no-checklist-items` drops a prompt and does **not** drop a unit, so under `tp run` a corpus role with an empty checklist costs a whole subagent process — context initialisation, brief, a `tp review <spec> --role <id>` invocation, an empty-file write, and a Stop-hook round-trip — to produce zero rows and record nothing. That is exactly the cost this release exists to remove (§4.3 prices bytes handed to units that read none of them), reproduced one level up at unit granularity, and it is the one place the spec buys surface without pricing it. §4.4 defers the `regression` gap on the ground that fixing it is *new* unit-lifecycle surface; this case is the opposite — applying an existing skip reason inside `roleUnits` removes a unit, it does not add a kind.
suggestion: Price it or close it. Either add one sentence to §4.2.1 or §4.4 stating that a `no-checklist-items` role still costs a full unit that reads and writes nothing, and naming who fixes it (as Non-Goals 5 and 6 do for the unowned questions); or state that `roleUnits` applies the `no-checklist-items` skip so no such unit is spawned. The exit-0 branch survives either choice untouched, because `no-spec-change` under `--diff-from` still diverges the unit set from the emitted set — so closing this loses nothing §4.2.1 argued for.

finding: §4.2.2 pins one ordering rule — the --role *refusal* is evaluated 'before the mode's own argument validation' — but says nothing about the other error interaction the release creates. §4.2.1's exit-2 case is not a refusal: it fires for a name tp recognises nowhere, and its hint must list 'what the invocation would have emitted', which requires actually computing the emission. For `tp audit <spec> --role bogus` on a clean tree, §7 measures that the emission is never computed (exit 4, no changed files). So the spec specifies exit 2 with a hint whose content is unobtainable, and does not say which exit code wins. An implementer must choose between three defensible behaviours (exit 4 first; exit 2 with an empty/degraded hint; exit 2 after forcing an affected-files scan) with no guidance, and checklist question 30 — the exact exit code an agent receives — has no answer for this path.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §4.2.1 or §4.2.2 fixing the precedence, e.g. 'Where the mode cannot compute an emission at all (tp audit with an empty changed-file set, exit 4), that failure is reported first; --role is validated only once an emission exists.' Then say what the exit-2 hint contains when the emitted set is empty for a legitimate reason, so the hint has a defined value in every case it can be produced.

finding:
Property 3's central term, "property 1's suffix", is never delimited by property 1, because property 1's ends-with predicate takes a construction whose first element is an operation rather than a byte string. Property 1: "ends with §2.3's construction exactly — trailing newline removed, then `LF LF`, §2.2's clause, `LF LF`, §3.2's clause, no trailing newline." §2.3's construction begins with `<the body as assembled before this release's append, trailing newline removed>`, so read literally "ends with the construction" is a statement about the entire body and is trivially true; read as intended it is a statement about a 468-byte tail that property 1 does not isolate and does not measure. Property 3 then hangs its whole discriminating comparison on that undefined term plus a constant that only §1.1's table derives. Property 3 itself concedes the defect one sentence later — "property 1's 'ends with' cannot see a byte removed before the suffix" — which is a statement that the first element of the construction is not part of any suffix. An engineer writing from property 1 alone has no way to know that the assertion is `HasSuffix(body, "

"+c2+"

"+c3)` and that its length is 468.
suggestion: Split the two into a named string and a separate strip clause: define **the suffix** once, in §2.3, as the byte string `LF LF` + §2.2's clause + `LF LF` + §3.2's clause, and state its length there. Property 1 then reads "ends with the suffix and does not end with a newline"; property 3 reads "the body with the suffix's length removed neither ends with the suffix nor ends with a newline", and no property has to name a construction that contains an operation.

finding: Property 4's 'Every other top-level key is unchanged' deliberately freezes `structured_elements` into the `--role` payload, and that key is duplicated content the recipient cannot act on. Measured on this round's emission: `structured_elements` is 2,295 bytes listing 7 tables and 22 numbered lists, and every one of those 29 entries is already restated in prose inside each prompt's own checklist — 'Check each of these specifically: 1. Table "1.1 What it costs" (line 36, 7 rows): apply your review lens to each row.' The unit acts on the prompt, never on the key. In the 179,854-byte panel the duplication is 1.3% and invisible; in the 25,062-byte single-role payload it is 9.2%. So the release shrinks what a unit receives by 90.6% and then pins the one key whose share that shrink multiplies sevenfold, which is the AX lens applied to the panel but not to what is left.
suggestion: Make it a priced decision rather than a silent one. Either have §4.2 drop `structured_elements` under `--role` — the prompt already carries the same inventory in the only form the unit reads, so nothing is lost — and let property 4's exception clause name it alongside `review_loop.instruction`; or keep it for cross-form stability and say so in §4.2 with the 1.3%→9.2% figure attached, so a later reader can see the trade was made rather than inherited.

finding: The release gate leaves one of its own inputs to the implementer, so two runs of the same gate can measure different sets and neither is wrong. §7 makes the gate §6.2 property 8 and then says of its `tp audit` half: "The gate supplies them with `--affected-files` or `--base <previous tag>`; which one is the implementer's." Property 8's scope is "every spec in the repository an unrestricted invocation emits prompts for" — a set that is a function of exactly that input, since the audit emission is derived from the affected files. So the gate's coverage is a free parameter, and the gate has no floor: an `--affected-files` value that yields no emitted prompts satisfies property 8 over the empty set and reports green, which is the same vacuity the paragraph's first half was written to close for the clean-tree case. A pass/fail gate whose subject set is chosen at run time cannot be re-run to the same verdict, and nothing records which input a given green was obtained with.
suggestion: Pin the input rather than the option: name `--base <previous release tag>` as the gate's audit input (deterministic, re-derivable from the tag, and the same for every operator), and add a floor to property 8 — the gate fails if the number of specs contributing at least one compared prompt is zero, or below the count §7 measures for the corpus — so an input that empties the subject set is reported as a gate failure rather than a pass.

finding: Non-Goal 7's last sentence repeats its second and ends the item on the shorter of the two lists. Sentence 2 already enumerates the exceptions — 'Two things do change and are named rather than hidden under "nothing": the two clauses §2 and §3 append, and `review_loop.instruction` under `--role` (§4.2.3.1)'. Sentence 3 then says 'The prompt does gain two behavioural clauses — that is §2 and §3, and §1 prices them; the claim here is narrower than "nothing changes"', which restates the first half of that list and adds only the pointer to §1's pricing. It reads as a leftover from the round before `review_loop.instruction` joined the exception list, and a reader who stops at the end of the item is left holding the two-item version of a three-item claim.
suggestion: Delete the last sentence and fold its only new content into sentence 2: '… the two clauses §2 and §3 append (§1.1 prices them), and `review_loop.instruction` under `--role` (§4.2.3.1).'

finding: This round's repair to Non-Goal 7 added a sentence enumerating the release's exceptions and left the sentence it supersedes in place, so the item now states one exception twice and the surviving older statement is the narrower, stale one. Non-Goal 7 reads: "The checklist items, role rules and output schema are untouched. Two things do change and are named rather than hidden under 'nothing': the two clauses §2 and §3 append, and `review_loop.instruction` under `--role` (§4.2.3.1). The prompt does gain two behavioural clauses — that is §2 and §3, and §1 prices them; the claim here is narrower than 'nothing changes'." The third sentence re-announces one of the two exceptions the second sentence has just enumerated, and its closing clause ("narrower than 'nothing changes'") repeats the second sentence's "rather than hidden under 'nothing'". The exception list is the thing this Non-Goal exists to keep exact — it was already short by one in round 14 — and it now has two edit sites with nothing marking the second, which is the drift §1.1 records four retired authoring rules for.
suggestion: Delete the third sentence, folding its only non-duplicated content into the second: "Two things do change and are named rather than hidden under 'nothing': the two clauses §2 and §3 append, which §1.1 prices, and `review_loop.instruction` under `--role` (§4.2.3.1)."
